seo.title: Karmic tail 3 16 13 compatibility in the destiny matrix
seo.description: Karmic tail 3 16 13 compatibility: the Empress at the entry, the Tower midway, Death as the main task and the Star at the centre, through The Winter's Tale.

title: The 3-16-13 karmic tail in compatibility: the Empress, the Tower and Death
short: The 3-16-13 karmic tail in a couple's destiny matrix looks like a verdict: the union enters its task through the Empress, passes through the Tower and runs into Death. Yet at the centre of every such couple stands the Star, a card that never appears at the centre of any one person's chart. In compatibility, the 3-16-13 karmic tail is not about the end of love but about the end of a portrait. The couple begins with a generous home and a beautiful picture of each other; halfway along the picture collapses; and the main task is not to turn to stone over the wreckage, but to meet the living, changed partner all over again.

sections.h2: The Winter's Tale: a play staged in the order 3-16-13
paragraphs: Shakespeare wrote it around 1610–1611. Leontes, King of Sicilia, and his wife Hermione have spent nine months hosting his childhood friend Polixenes, King of Bohemia. The guest is ready to leave; Leontes cannot keep him and asks his wife. Hermione wins him over in a minute. From that minute Leontes is jealous, without a single piece of evidence: he declares his wife an adulteress, has his newborn daughter carried off to a desert place and puts the queen on trial. Apollo's oracle answers that Hermione is chaste and Leontes a jealous tyrant. The king refuses to believe the oracle, and at once the news comes that his little son is dead. Hermione is carried out senseless, and Paulina, her friend, declares the queen dead.

Then Time comes on stage and turns his glass: sixteen years have passed. The abandoned girl has grown up with a shepherd in Bohemia, her name is Perdita, and the son of Polixenes is in love with her. The lovers flee to Sicilia, everything comes to light, and in the last scene Paulina takes the king to see a statue of the late queen. The statue breathes. Hermione had been alive all sixteen years.

The play has a draft by another hand: Robert Greene's romance Pandosto (1588). The plot is almost the same, the cards are the same, and the ending is different. The article will come back to it at the end, because the difference between the two books is the main task of this tail. Shakespeare is quoted in the original throughout.

sections.h2: The Empress at the entry: "Our praises are our wages"
paragraphs: The play opens with plenty. The guest's first words are a count of time: "Nine changes of the watery star hath been / The shepherd's note since we have left our throne / Without a burden." Nine months of hospitality, and the lady of the house is heavily pregnant. Waite opens the Empress's list with the word **"Fruitfulness"**, and Shakespeare puts her on stage quite literally.

Leontes asks his guest to stay one week more, and the guest refuses. So the king turns to his wife: "Tongue-tied, our queen? Speak you." Hermione sets about it gaily and with authority: "My prisoner or my guest?" Polixenes gives in: "Your guest, then, madam." — "Not your gaoler then, / But your kind hostess." The king drops a short line aside: "At my request he would not." And Hermione asks for her reward: "Cram's with praise, and make's / As fat as tame things… Our praises are our wages."

Wen writes that the Empress suggests "an incredible gift for harnessing interpersonal relationships to yield success and harmony". That is Hermione's gift exactly. And the same gift becomes the first crack: Leontes himself names her qualities, admitting that such welcome may "derive a liberty / From heartiness, from bounty, fertile bosom", allows that it may be innocent, and does not believe it.

The couple's point M is the entry to the task: shared wishes, agreements, a common language. It is no accident that the same point also sits on the relationship line of the couple's matrix, where its caption is "Common language". For a 3-16-13 couple that language is plenty: a full house, gifts, feasts, praise as currency. But the point lies on the line of tasks, and Lisovskaya warns that what a couple wants can turn into resistance. The Empress's mechanism is simple: plenty always spills outwards. The more generous one partner is with others, the easier it is for the other to start keeping score.

A scene from life. He asked her himself to invite their colleagues and to be welcoming. She was. The guests stayed until one in the morning, someone said in the hallway, "It's so lovely here, I don't want to leave," and in the taxi he is silent until finally: "You never laugh like that with me." The line "At my request he would not" is of the same kind: the request was granted, and the sour taste stayed with the one who asked. Or another scene: praise has become a salary, and a week without it feels like wages paid late. The roles are open here: either partner can be the welcoming one, and either can be the one counting.

This wish has a hidden condition, and Shakespeare spells it out. Polixenes remembers his boyhood with Leontes: "Two lads that thought there was no more behind / But such a day tomorrow as today, / And to be boy eternal." The Empress at the entry wants plenty to last forever. That is why Death stands as the couple's main task: that very "forever" has to be given up.

sections.h2: The Tower in the middle: "With what's unreal thou coactive art"
paragraphs: While Hermione talks and laughs with the guest, Leontes speaks a monologue in which Shakespeare describes the mechanism with textbook precision: "Affection! thy intention stabs the centre: / Thou dost make possible things not so held, / Communicat'st with dreams;—how can this be?— / With what's unreal thou coactive art." Passion works hand in hand with what does not exist.

The portrait is built quickly and in silence, and from then on everything becomes evidence. A whisper, a glance, hand in hand: "Is this nothing? / Why, then the world and all that's in't is nothing, / The covering sky is nothing, Bohemia nothing, / My wife is nothing." At the trial Hermione speaks the line that explains the whole middle of this tail: "My life stands in the level of your dreams." Leontes replies: "Your actions are my dreams."

The oracle tells the truth. The king: "There is no truth at all i' th' oracle." A minute later comes the news of his son, and Leontes names the blow himself: "Apollo's angry, and the heavens themselves / Do strike at my injustice." And straight after: **"I have too much believ'd mine own suspicion."** This is where the Tower's lightning strikes: not at the moment of the accusation, but at the moment the portrait crumbles and underneath it stands a living person nobody had been looking at.

Among a couple's tasks under the Tower, Lisovskaya lists, in so many words, **the collapse of an invented image of the partner**. For the 3-16-13 tail this is the main key to the middle of the path. The portrait can be dark: a story that the partner has gone cold, is hiding something, is playing a game. It can be bright: "he's made of iron," "she never gets tired," "we never fight." The bright one falls just like the dark one: in a single evening, when the man of iron says "I can't do this any more" and the one who never gets tired says no for the first time. The feeling is the same: "I don't know who this is." That is the Tower: not trouble from outside, but a picture caving in from within.

The numbers add a clue the play does not have. The middle of a couple's tail is the sum of the middles of two personal tails. In every 3-16-13 couple it is **the Emperor of one partner (4) and the Hanged Man of the other (12)**. In Waite's list the Emperor stands for "Stability, power, protection… also authority and will", the Hanged Man for "Wisdom, circumspection… trials, sacrifice". Both halves are visible in the play. One rules alone, and Hermione names it precisely: "'Tis rigour, and not law." The other endures: "There's some ill planet reigns: / I must be patient till the heavens look / With an aspect more favourable." A verdict without a question plus patience without a word brings the house down. Neither half builds the Tower alone; their sum does. Which of the two is the Emperor and which the Hanged Man does not depend on gender, and in a couple's life they change places.

One more detail from Waite: among the old titles of the Tower he lists "Castle of Plutus", the castle of the god of wealth. A couple that entered its task through the Empress's plenty meets, halfway along, lightning in the castle of wealth. And Wen, writing on the reversed Tower, comes close to describing Hermione: the Seeker has been falsely accused, yet "not all will be destroyed. There will be mercy and some will be saved." In the play, it is the girl who is saved.

One caveat, in all seriousness. If suspicion in a couple turns into surveillance, threats or fear for one's safety, this is no longer a matter for the cards and no reason to wait sixteen years: it calls for a psychologist and, in danger, a local emergency number or crisis line.

sections.h2: Death as the main task: sixteen years of two statues
paragraphs: After the trial Leontes makes a vow: "Once a day I'll visit / The chapel where they lie, and tears shed there / Shall be my recreation." Time, as chorus, leafs through sixteen years in a few lines: "I turn my glass, and give my scene such growing / As you had slept between." All this while the king grieves alone. Hermione, whom everyone believes dead, lives hidden in Paulina's house.

Here the couple's arithmetic is at work again. The Hanged Man, who always stands in the middle of one partner's personal tail, is described by Waite like this: the figure, as a whole, suggests **"life in suspension, but life and not death"**. Nothing could describe Hermione's sixteen years more exactly. And in the last act Camillo says of Leontes: "My lord, your sorrow was too sore laid on, / Which sixteen winters cannot blow away, / So many summers dry. Scarce any joy / Did ever so long live; no sorrow / But kill'd itself much sooner." Ordinary grief buries itself. This one did not.

The couple's main task, point D, is read mostly through its minus: what does not work for the couple and what it has to learn. For the 3-16-13 tail the trap is not the collapse itself but what comes after. The couple stays together but lives "as if": one keeps apologising for years after being forgiven; the other keeps a locked room inside. Nothing in the house changes, the anniversary is marked in the same restaurant, they talk mostly about the past. Waite's reversed Death includes "petrifaction"; Wen's speaks of a plateau, when it is time to move into a new phase and letting go of the old one will not happen. In the play these are two statues: one on the pedestal, the other in front of it.

Among a couple's tasks under Death, Lisovskaya names **a partner quite unlike the previous one, and the rejection of that difference**. In the 3-16-13 tail the "previous one" is often the very same person, as they were before the collapse. Our reading: the partner is compared with their own portrait from ten years ago, and so the invented image survives even the Tower. In the same place Lisovskaya speaks of living through crises as a test and seeing one's own mistakes, not only the other's. Leontes saw his mistake at once; it took him sixteen years to leave the tomb.

The main task itself is also made of two personal ones: the Wheel of Fortune (10), the karmic task of one partner, plus the Empress (3), the karmic task of the other. Two personal tasks add up to one shared task: Death.

sections.h2: "Be stone no more": what Death really does
paragraphs: Paulina draws back the curtain. The king recognises his wife's posture, and at once notices not the miracle but her age: "But yet, Paulina, / Hermione was not so much wrinkled, nothing / So aged as this seems." Paulina answers: "So much the more our carver's excellence, / Which lets go by some sixteen years and makes her / As she liv'd now." And Leontes makes the central confession of the play: **"does not the stone rebuke me / For being more stone than it?"** Both of them had turned to stone.

Then music sounds, and Paulina speaks to the statue: "'Tis time; descend; be stone no more; approach; / Strike all that look upon with marvel. Come; / I'll fill your grave up: stir; nay, come away. / Bequeath to death your numbness, for from him / Dear life redeems you." Bequeath to death your numbness. This is the exact formula of the tail's main task: what is handed over to death is not love and not the person, but the stone. Death in this tail takes away a form that has stopped living and frees those who froze inside it.

What comes back is not the old marriage. Hermione steps down from the pedestal and comes to her husband herself, while Paulina urges the king to offer his hand: when she was young he courted her; must she, now in age, do the courting? ("When she was young you woo'd her; now in age / Is she become the suitor?") The roles have shifted: this time the first step is taken by the other. On the very day of the lightning Leontes had promised to "New woo my queen"; now the courtship begins again. Hermione embraces her husband but says not a word to him: her first words are for her daughter. An honest ending: the new begins not with a talk about the past, but with an embrace and a different story.

Shakespeare packed the whole Death card into one line, at the hinge of the play, in the same scene as his famous stage direction "Exit, pursued by a bear." The old shepherd says to his son: **"thou met'st with things dying, I with things new-born."** Wen recalls that traditionally this card is related to "death and birth" at once. Waite writes of a mystical death while still in this life, which is "a change in the form of consciousness". And Perdita, kneeling before the statue, addresses her mother: "Dear queen, that ended when I but began."

The strong version of the 3-16-13 tail is a couple that has buried a portrait and not each other. In Lisovskaya's description, from outside such couples look like living proof that life goes on after something hard; inside, they accept the partner's past and take the partner's changes in their stride. Paulina warns that if they were only told she lives, it "should be hooted at / Like an old tale", and Leontes answers the miracle in everyday terms: "If this be magic, let it be an art / Lawful as eating." There is no magic in this tail. There is work, as ordinary as eating: getting to know, each time, the person who is there now.

sections.h2: The Star at the couple's centre: hope that is not put on show
paragraphs: The centre of the matrix in every 3-16-13 couple is **17, the Star**, in one hundred per cent of cases. In a personal matrix a centre of 17 never occurs, for any date: only a couple creates this card at the centre. It is made of the two personal centres: Strength (11) of one partner and the Lovers (6) of the other. In Waite's lists Strength includes "magnanimity" and the Lovers "trials overcome". The magnanimity of one plus the trials that the other's love came through add up to hope.

The couple's centre is the atmosphere inside the couple: what happens between the two of them when nobody is watching. In the play, too, hope is hidden. Paulina says of the statue: "therefore I keep it / Lonely, apart." At the end Hermione explains what kept her going for sixteen years: "Knowing by Paulina that the oracle / Gave hope thou wast in being, have preserv'd / Myself to see the issue." The word the oracle gave her was hope, that her daughter was alive. One word of hope, and sixteen years of life behind a curtain.

Wen writes that "The Star card appears chronologically in the Major Arcana after a great deal of pain: The Hanged Man, Death, The Devil, and The Tower", and that it signals "the final low point in a situation has passed". In a 3-16-13 couple that whole sequence is present: the Tower in the middle of the tail for all of them, Death as the main task for all of them, the Hanged Man in the middle of one partner's personal tail for all of them, the Devil in the values for 28.2%. Only the Star stands not at the end of the path, as in the deck, but at the centre. For this couple hope is not a reward after the trials; it is what was inside all along.

In Lisovskaya, the Star in a couple's atmosphere is that rare case when the pretty picture turns out to be true. Its minus is fitting the partner to one's own image. Even the centre of this tail speaks to the same dispute: the living picture against the invented one. Such couples usually do not say their hope out loud; they keep it the way Paulina keeps the statue, behind a curtain. It is worth showing it to each other now and then.

On the Star card of the Waite–Smith deck (the picture on our site is different), a naked woman "pours Water of Life from two great ewers, irrigating sea and land". Waite writes that for the majority of prepared minds the figure will appear as **"the type of Truth unveiled, glorious in undying beauty"**.

In the last scene of The Winter's Tale the truth is unveiled literally: "Paulina undraws a curtain, and discovers Hermione standing as a statue." And the first words of the revived queen repeat the gesture of Waite's card: "You gods, look down, / And from your sacred vials pour your graces / Upon my daughter's head!" Pour from your sacred vessels.

Waite's divinatory list for the Star opens unexpectedly: "Loss, theft, privation, abandonment; another reading says—hope and bright prospects". Loss and hope in one card. In Shakespeare they are one girl. Antigonus, carrying the infant to a desert shore, sees Hermione in a dream, and she asks: "for the babe / Is counted lost for ever, Perdita / I prithee call't." Perdita is Latin for "lost". At the trial her mother calls her "Starr'd most unluckily". The oracle sets a condition: the king shall live without an heir "if that which is lost be not found". The lost one turns out to be the hope.

One last detail. Waite's Star "expresses eternal youth and beauty", while Hermione steps down from the pedestal sixteen years older. Hope in this tail does not keep a face young. It keeps a person alive.

sections.h2: The couple's values: the Lovers or the Devil
paragraphs: The couple's values are its spiritual purpose, what the union exists for. In 3-16-13 couples there are two variants: **the Lovers (6) in 71.8%** and **the Devil (15) in 28.2%**.

In the play the Lovers are played by the second generation. Florizel, son of Polixenes, chooses a shepherd girl against his father's will: "From my succession wipe me, father; I / Am heir to my affection." It is the lovers' flight that brings everyone to Sicilia, to the statue: the children's union untangles the parents' story. For a couple with the Lovers in its values, the union exists for a choice made again and again, not one inherited along with old scripts. Waite's list for this card holds those very "trials overcome".

With the Devil the picture is different. Lisovskaya's final thought on the fifteenth energy in a couple is that **nobody belongs to anybody**. Leontes's Tower grew out of a question of ownership: "Mamillius, / Art thou my boy?" he asks, and checks the boy's nose against his own: "They say it is a copy out of mine." In couples with the Devil in the values, three cards of the deck stand in a row: the Devil (15) in the values, the Tower (16) in the middle of the tail, the Star (17) at the centre. Waite links the neighbours himself: "There is a sense in which the catastrophe is a reflection from the previous card." The task of such couples is passion and a strong bond without any right of ownership.

sections.h2: Two endings of one plot: Pandosto and The Winter's Tale
paragraphs: Greene's romance came out in 1588 under the title Pandosto. The Triumph of Time. The title page promises to show "that although by the means of sinister fortune Truth may be concealed, yet by Time in spite of fortune it is most manifestly revealed" (Greene is quoted here and below in modernised spelling), and carries the motto Temporis filia veritas, "Truth is the daughter of Time".

The plot is the same: a jealous king, a friend's flight, an oracle, a son's death, an abandoned daughter, and years later, young lovers. But Bellaria, Greene's queen, really dies: she "could be never revived". And at the end the king, remembering how he betrayed his friend, how his jealousy caused his wife's death and how he desired his own daughter without knowing her, kills himself, "to close up the Comedy with a Tragical stratagem".

Shakespeare left the cards where they were and changed one thing: the reading of Death. In Greene it is an end; in Shakespeare, a passage. He kept Time too, and even gave him a part, but his Time declines to tell fortunes: "What of her ensues / I list not prophesy; but let Time's news / Be known when 'tis brought forth." A 3-16-13 couple holds both books. The cards do not choose the ending. They show where the choice lies: whether it is the portrait that gets buried, or the person.

sections.h2: How the 3-16-13 karmic tail is calculated in compatibility: a sample couple
paragraphs: The example is a couple born on 14.10.1975 and 19.03.1979; the calculation was checked by the site's engine. First each partner's personal matrix is built.

ul: **19.03.1979.** Day 19, month 3, year 1 + 9 + 7 + 9 = 26 → 8. Karmic task: 19 + 3 + 8 = 30 → 3. Centre: 19 + 3 + 8 + 3 = 33 → 6. Entry of the tail: 3 + 6 = 9, middle: 3 + 9 = 12. Personal tail: 9-12-3.

paragraphs: Each point of the couple is the sum of the same points of the two personal matrices, reduced to 22 or less:

The couple's middle is not recalculated from the two outer numbers: it is the sum of the partners' middles, 4 + 12. That 3 + 13 also gives 16 here is a coincidence of this particular tail, not the way to count. This couple's values are 15, the Devil: it belongs to the 28.2%. Lisovskaya advises checking whether the same energies stand on other points, and here they do: Death also stands in "What to create together", the Tower in "Where it sparks", the Star in "What connects".
Three facts about the tail, checked by running through every date:

ul: **3-16-13 occurs in about one couple in 137** (0.729%), 47th place out of 97 couple tails.

**It is built from only one combination of personal tails: 21-4-10 in one partner and 9-12-3 in the other**, in one hundred per cent of such couples. If a couple has this tail, the partners' personal tails can be named in advance.

**3-16-13 never occurs as a personal tail.** In a personal matrix the entry equals the karmic task plus the centre: with a task of 13 and an entry of 3 the centre would have to be 17, and no person has such a centre. There are no other couple tails made of the numbers 3, 16 and 13: this order is the only one.

sections.h2: What helps a couple with the 3-16-13 tail

ul: **Say the portrait out loud.** When a story about the partner starts to take shape ("gone cold", "hiding something", "he'd never give up"), voice it as a guess and ask, rather than making up the rest. Leontes did ask the oracle, but he did not ask in order to hear.

**Do not judge alone, and do not endure in silence.** This couple's Tower is built from one partner's power and the other's wordless patience. A verdict without a question and patience without a word bring the house down alike.
**Praise each other, not only in front of guests.** The Empress lives on praise, and generosity to strangers hurts the one who got none of it at home.
**After a crisis, build a new way of living, not a shrine.** Change the agreements, the routines, the roles: who leads and who courts. Visiting the same tomb every day is also a choice.
**Get acquainted again.** Compare the partner not with who they were before the collapse but with who they are now. The statue's wrinkles are not a reproach but sixteen years lived.

**Now and then, bring hope out from behind the curtain.** The Star at the centre of this couple is a quiet one. Telling each other what one still hopes for is Paulina's gesture, only without the sixteen years of waiting.

intro: The three points of the tail are read from the entry to the main task, and each has its own role:

ul: **3 · The Empress — entry to the task.** The couple's shared wish is a warm, generous house that guests never want to leave, and a common language of praise. The point sits on the line of tasks, so the same wish turns into resistance: generosity towards others breeds comparison.

**16 · The Tower — middle of the task.** The couple's path runs through the collapse of an invented image of the partner, dark or bright, it makes no difference. What falls is the portrait, not the person.
**13 · Death — main task.** To let the old shape of the union go and not freeze inside it for years: to meet the partner as they have become, and to start courting again.

intro: Shakespeare wrote this plot down four hundred years ago. The Winter's Tale runs exactly in the order 3-16-13: a palace of plenty where a pregnant queen persuades a guest to stay; a jealousy that strikes like lightning; sixteen years in which the wife is thought dead and the husband weeps at her tomb every day; and the scene in which the queen's statue steps down from its pedestal. What follows is an investigation: what lies in the cards themselves, in the books of Waite, Wen and Lisovskaya, and in the site engine's run through every date.

faq.q: What does the 3-16-13 karmic tail mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is a couple's task that begins with plenty and a generous home (the Empress at the entry), passes through the collapse of an invented image of the partner (the Tower in the middle) and asks the couple to let the old shape of the union go without turning to stone inside it (Death as the main task). At the centre of such couples there is always the Star: a quiet hope that holds the union from within.

faq.q: Does 3-16-13 occur in a personal destiny matrix?
faq.a: No. In a personal matrix the entry of the tail equals the karmic task plus the centre, and a task of 13 with an entry of 3 would need a centre of 17, which no person has. So a search for "3 16 13 in the destiny matrix" is always about a couple's matrix: this tail appears only when two dates are added together.

faq.q: Does the 3-16-13 tail mean the couple will break up?
faq.a: No. Death as the main task speaks of the end of a form, not of the union: what dies is the old way of living and the old portrait of each other. The tail does not predict events or dates; it shows what the couple goes through and where its choice lies. Even Time in Shakespeare declines to prophesy.

faq.q: Which partner is Leontes and which is Hermione?
faq.a: Neither, for good. The play's roles are not divided by gender and not assigned forever: either partner can build the portrait, and either can freeze in patience. The numbers suggest only one thing: the middle of the tail is made of one partner's Emperor and the other's Hanged Man, so the collapse is always shared.

faq.q: Are there couple tails with the same numbers in another order?
faq.a: No. Among the 97 couple tails the numbers 3, 16 and 13 occur only in this order: the Empress at the entry, the Tower in the middle, Death as the main task. Order matters here: the three numbers are read from the entry to the task towards the main task.

And he confesses: **"does not the stone rebuke me / For being more stone than it?"** Both of them had turned to stone. Paulina commands the statue: "be stone no more… / Bequeath to death your numbness, for from him / Dear life redeems you." What is handed to death is not love but numbness. What comes back is not the old marriage: the wife steps down from the pedestal and comes to her husband herself, and the courtship begins again, with the first step taken by the other. Halfway through the play the old shepherd had said it in one line: "thou met'st with things dying, I with things new-born."

Shakespeare had a model: Greene's romance Pandosto, where the same plot ends with the death of both the queen and the king. Shakespeare changed one thing, the reading of Death: from an end it became a passage. **The cards do not choose the ending. They show where the choice lies: whether it is the portrait that gets buried, or the person.**

The Star at the couple's centre is the atmosphere inside the couple: what happens between the two of them when nobody is watching. It is made of the two personal centres, Strength of one partner and the Lovers of the other. Wen places the Star in the deck after a great deal of pain: the Hanged Man, Death, the Devil, the Tower. In a 3-16-13 couple these cards are close at hand, but the Star stands not at the end of the path but inside it: here hope is not a reward after the trials, it is what was in the couple all along.

In the play hope is hidden: the statue is kept "Lonely, apart", behind a curtain. Hermione lived sixteen years on a single phrase of the oracle, which "Gave hope" that her daughter was alive. The daughter is called Perdita, Latin for "lost", and Waite's divinatory list for the Star also opens with loss and goes on to hope.

The strong version of this tail is a couple that has buried a portrait and not each other. It says its guesses about the partner out loud instead of making up the rest. It does not judge alone and does not endure in silence. It compares the partners not with who they were before the collapse, but with the people there now. And now and then it brings hope out from behind the curtain, without the sixteen years of waiting.
